introduction: What happens in prayer? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s answers are simple and repeated: it is conversation with God, the speech of one who loves, a state more than a form of words, and “the heart is enough.” The readings go on to its conditions (attention, humility, the freedom of the heart from distraction and from self), its times, the ablutions, the individual character of the obligatory prayer and the reserve about formal congregational prayer, and the question of where the mind should turn. They end with surrender and with action: “look unto its means.” The Psalms are prayer’s oldest school and appear throughout, with the Gospels’ teaching on prayer in secret, Hannah’s silent lips, Daniel’s open windows, Nehemiah’s prayer and watch, the Mishnah’s hour of preparation, the Qur’án, Rábi‘a, Rúmí, Herbert, Johnson, Ignatius and a Dakota account of worship without set times. Emerson rejects petition altogether, Tagore calls the worshipper out of the temple, the second commandment stands against any pictured object, and “two or three gathered together” speaks for prayer in company.
questions: “If there is anyone that you love do you not seek an opportunity to speak with him?” How does thinking of prayer as a lover’s speech change what one says, and how often?
“Words are not necessary, the heart is enough,” and yet there are obligatory prayers with fixed words. What does each do that the other cannot?
The Báb says that to find one’s own desire in prayer is to associate a partner with God; Emerson calls petition “vicious”; the readings still tell people to ask. What is the right place of asking?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of holding “some object” in mind and of turning to Bahá’u’lláh; a later letter advises letting a mental image fade into qualities. How do you understand the centre toward which prayer turns?
Obligatory prayer is private and formal congregational prayer is set aside, yet singing and praying together are encouraged. What is the difference the readings are protecting?
“Look unto its means,” and Nehemiah prayed and set a watch. Think of something you have prayed for. What were its means?

outside.why: “There is a pleasure in offering prayers that transcends all other pleasures.” A psalm: as the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
Prayer is “conversation with God.” Tennyson: speak to Him thou for He hears, and Spirit with Spirit can meet; closer is He than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet.
George Herbert’s sonnet piles up names for it and ends on the plainest: God’s breath in man returning to his birth; something understood.
A friend who loves “will wish to say so,” though the other knows. The risen Jesus asked Peter three times, and Peter answered: Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee.

Why pray, if God knows? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s answer is love. Jesus states the premise as a warning: your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him. What kinds of prayer does that knowledge rule out, and what kind does it leave?
Obligatory prayer makes “a connection between the servant and the True One.” A psalm: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee.
Supplication “is by itself a light to his heart”; “when the vessel is widened the water” increases. Jesus: ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find.
Augustine on why the asking is itself the gift: thou hast made us for thyself, and our heart is restless until it rests in thee.
“Supplication and prayer is the Water of Life.” Jesus at the well: the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
“Prayer confers spirituality upon the heart.” Of Moses after forty days of converse on the mountain it is said that the skin of his face shone, and he did not know it.
“There is no state like the state of prayer.” The Mishnah on preparing for it: the pious men of old used to wait an hour before praying in order that they might direct their thoughts to God.
Prayer “is both attitude and word … like a song.” Paul: we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
“Words are not necessary, the heart is enough.” Hannah at Shiloh: she spake in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard.
Rúmí has God rebuke Moses for correcting a shepherd’s clumsy prayer: I regard not the outside and the words, I regard the inside and the state of heart.
“One must live in a perennial attitude of prayer.” Paul: pray without ceasing.
The mind the altar, the heart the sanctuary. Jesus: the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth.
A prayer that shall “rise above words and letters.” A psalm: be still, and know that I am God.

Charles Eastman on the Dakota worship in which he was raised: the hunter comes upon a scene strikingly beautiful or sublime, and pauses for an instant in the attitude of worship. He sees no need for setting apart one day in seven, since to him all days are God’s.
“Thou hearest my crying in the depths of night.” A psalm: O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.
“It is incumbent upon every servant to pray … and implore.” Jesus told a parable to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
Recite it “with utmost humility.” The prayer Jesus commended: God be merciful to me a sinner.
“Commune with Him at midnight.” A psalm: at midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee.
Jesus: he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.
“Now is the hour for beseeching and supplicating Him.” Paul: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

Say the prayers “as much as thou art able, so that day by day thou mayest attain to increased firmness.” Daniel under a decree that forbade it: he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, as he did aforetime.
“The highest and most elevating state is the state of prayer.” Mark: rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.

Its efficacy depends on a heart free of “extraneous suggestions.” Emerson went further and condemned asking for anything at all: prayer that craves a particular commodity is vicious; prayer is the contemplation of the facts of life from the highest point of view. Do the readings agree that petition is a lower form, or do they keep it?

“When you pray you must not think of your aching body, nor of the birds outside the window.” The king in Hamlet rises from his knees: my words fly up, my thoughts remain below: words without thoughts never to heaven go.
A lover cannot keep from mentioning the beloved’s name. Peter and John: we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

The supplicant should “behold none but the countenance of his Lord”; to find his own desire there is to set up a partner. Rábi‘a of Basra: whatever share of this world Thou hast allotted to me, bestow it on Thine enemies. Thou art enough for me.

“If healing is right for the patient, it will certainly be granted”; for some it would bring other ills. Samuel Johnson: still raise for good the supplicating voice, but leave to Heaven the measure and the choice.
The model of such prayer: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.

Some prayers are not granted, in wisdom. James gives a blunter reason for some refusals: ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts. How would a person know which explanation applies to a prayer of his own?
“When thou prayest to God for any need, look unto its means.” Nehemiah, rebuilding a wall under threat: we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night.
God grants through means, and expects the asker to use them. Benjamin Franklin’s Poor Richard put it as a proverb: God helps them that help themselves.
Obligatory prayer is “to be performed by each of you individually.” Jesus: when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá states the objection, “I can pray to God whenever I wish … Why should I go where others are gathered?” and answers it. Jesus gave gathering a promise of its own: where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them. How do the readings hold together the private obligatory prayer and the value of praying in company?

“Congregational prayer has no spiritual attraction. Much hypocrisy enters into it.” The first Christians are remembered as continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, with gladness and singleness of heart. What is it in led, formal congregational prayer that the readings distrust, and what kind of praying together do the later letters allow?
“Prayer without ablution is impossible.” The Qur’án: when ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows.
“Supplication without humility is unacceptable.” A psalm: who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
While washing the face: “Illumine it with the light of Thy countenance.” A psalm: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
The prayer is said in the morning, at noon and in the evening. The Qur’án: worship at fixed times hath been enjoined on the believers.
In prayer one “should see himself severed from all created things.” Moses was told before he could listen: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Bahá’u’lláh is “the center towards whom all the faces are turned.” Jesus: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.

“At the time of prayer one must hold in one’s mind some object.” The second commandment forbids the making of any likeness for worship: thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image. How do the later letters, which advise letting a mental picture fade into qualities, guard against what the commandment fears?
“If we turn to God we must direct our hearts to a certain center.” Philip asked to be shown the Father, and Jesus answered: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
“Love, work, prayer, peace and joy.” Coleridge’s mariner: he prayeth best, who loveth best all things both great and small.
The Manifestation continues “to be our means of contact with the Almighty.” The First Letter to Timothy: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men.
“We cannot know God directly, but only through His Prophets.” John: no man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, he hath declared him.
We may pray to Bahá’u’lláh, or through him to God. Jesus: whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

Prayer through an intermediary is called more effective. The Qur’án insists on a nearness that needs none: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein. If God is that near, what is the Manifestation’s part in a person’s prayer?
In true worship “the worshipper and the words of worship are annihilated.” Paul: I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
“Before every endeavour … must we begin with prayer,” to commend ourselves to a Power already near. Proverbs: in all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Singing together in a House of Worship is welcomed. A psalm: sing unto the Lord a new song, and his praise in the congregation of saints.
Prayers that seem unanswered should not undermine faith. Habakkuk: although the fig tree shall not blossom, yet I will rejoice in the Lord.
Paul asked three times for relief and was given a different answer: my grace is sufficient for thee.
“His will should be completely submissive to the Will of God.” Ignatius of Loyola: take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my intellect, and all my will.
To be a reed through which the Spirit may flow. Milton, blind and unable to work as he had: they also serve who only stand and wait.

The letter goes on to insist that prayer be joined to action. Tagore says it sharply to the worshipper in the shut temple: leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground. What do the readings say prayer gives to work, that work alone does not have?
